newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU wheat export commitments near nine mln tonnes.
newsitem.headline: EU wheat export commitments near nine mln tonnes.

text.p: European Union soft wheat export commitments are approaching nine million tonnes following Thursday's tender, and the current campaign has about three quarters of a million tonnes left to run before attention switches to the next crop, grain traders said on Friday.

The EU on Thursday granted 480,000 tonnes of soft wheat exports, reducing a shortage of licences felt by the trade but keeping talk of an export licence squeeze alive as one company snatched up to two thirds of the volume, traders said.

The latest award -- less in volume terms than many traders had hoped for given a two-week gap in the auction process for the Easter holiday -- comes on top of 8.427 million tonnes committed between the start of the season last July 1 and March 18, EU data show.
"We can't complain too much, but they could have done a bit more," said a senior trader of the latest award, which capped refunds at 9.3 Ecus per tonne after aggressive bidding.

"The question is what are these guys going to do with half a million tonnes of wheat at $160 per tonne (the estimated world market value of the top refund when results were announced)," said another European trader.
Exporters said the volume given seemed to absorb much of the remaining short position following a series of potentially loss-making sales in the low $140s per tonne early this year.
But the market was not yet back in balance, with many of the licences held by a handful of companies and markets gearing up for a potentially damaging race for licences in April and May.

Wheat tenders are thin on the ground for the next few weeks, especially after this week's soybean-led rally, but Algeria and one or two others need some quantities despite Algeria's refusal to accept bids at this week's abandoned tender, traders said.

Traders were still puzzling over Algeria's reported refusal to deal with French companies at the tender for 75,000 tonnes of wheat. Most cited politics for the move but traders looked in vain for further confirmation trade relations were under threat.

Algeria reacted sharply to French Prime Minister Alain Juppe's call for a "democratic conscience" in France's violence-racked former colony, but an Algerian embassy official in Paris denied trade reports of a ban on French companies.
The official, however, said Algeria was not seeking to renew its French Coface and other grain credits for the time being.

The implied value of French wheat fluctuated either side of $160 per tonne after Thursday's EU tender and at one point slid below U.S. soft red winter as soybeans surged and the dollar strengthened on Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's warnings about the potential for inflationary pressures.
Currency dealers took the remarks as a pointer to a possible rise in U.S. interest rates, perhaps as early as next week.

Traders said the gap between old-crop and new-crop wheat prices in the U.S. might hamper new demand for several weeks, but some were ready to gamble on a further rise in prices caused by flooding, sowing uncertainty and a hotch-potch of logistical problems elsewhere.
"How much is left for the EU to do? I'd say one million looks optimistic, but maybe something between 700,000 tonnes and a million tonnes," said one French trader.

The EU, which started the season late but has caught up relatively well since, would end the July/June season with commercial soft wheat sales of slightly less than 10 million tonnes and flour sales just over five million tonnes, he said.
After a double refund cut in early March, flour export commitments have stalled in the past two weeks and stood at 5.040 million tonnes on March 18, EU figures showed.
